 Virginia’s Highland County Christmas Tree Headed to White House for National Holiday Celebration
 Published
 38 seconds ago on
 November 19, 2026 
 By
 Mike McCool 
 A red spruce that grew high in Virginia’s Highland County will soon become one of the most photographed Christmas trees in America.
 The 36-foot tree, selected from the George Washington and Jefferson National Forests, will serve as the 2026 National Christmas Tree on the Ellipse just south of the White House in Washington, D.C.
 The tree will be illuminated during the annual National Christmas Tree Lighting Ceremony on Thursday, December 3, and will be open to the public for viewing beginning December 5.
 On November 15, staff from the James River and Warm Springs Ranger Districts joined the National Park Service in Highland County, Virginia, to select the 2026 National Christmas Tree.
 For Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley and surrounding mountain communities, the selection brings national attention to the region’s forests and natural beauty.
 U.S. Rep. Ben Cline, who represents Virginia’s Sixth Congressional District, welcomed the announcement on November 19.
 “I am incredibly proud that a tree from Virginia’s Sixth Congressional District will represent our Commonwealth as the National Christmas Tree,” Cline said. “The Highlands are home to some of the most beautiful natural landscapes in the country, and this is a wonderful opportunity to showcase that beauty and heritage on a national stage.”
 From Highland County to the Nation’s Capital 
 A blanket of snow covers the mountains of Highland County, Virginia, on the day a 36-foot red spruce selected as this year’s National Christmas Tree was harvested. (USDA Forest Service photo by Preston Keres)
 Employees of the Forest Service’s James River and Warm Springs Ranger Districts selected the red spruce on November 15, working with the National Park Service.
 The tree came from the high-elevation forests of Highland County, one of Virginia’s most rural and mountainous areas.
 This marks the fourth year the Forest Service and National Park Service have partnered to provide the National Christmas Tree and the third consecutive year that the George Washington and Jefferson National Forests have contributed to the celebration.
 Acting Forest Supervisor Troy Morris said the selection offers a chance to share Virginia’s mountain heritage with the country.
 “We are honored to share this magnificent red spruce with the nation as the National Christmas Tree and to showcase the natural beauty and heritage of Virginia on a national stage,” Morris said.
 The red spruce is native to the Appalachian Mountains, particularly cooler, higher-elevation forests. Once more widespread in the region, red spruce populations were reduced by extensive historical logging and other environmental changes.
 Today, the Forest Service and conservation partners are working to restore these important mountain ecosystems.
 One restoration project near Mount Rogers calls for planting as many as 8,000 red spruce seedlings in early 2027, using seeds collected locally to help preserve the species.
 The selection of the National Christmas Tree highlights both the beauty of these forests and the continuing work to protect them.
 A Christmas Tradition More Than a Century Old 
 The National Christmas Tree Lighting Ceremony officially began on Christmas Eve in 1923, when President Calvin Coolidge illuminated a 48-foot balsam fir from Vermont.
 That tree was decorated with 2,500 red, white, and green electric bulbs, creating a holiday tradition that continues today.
 But Washington’s history of public Christmas tree celebrations actually reaches back another decade.
 On Christmas Eve in 1913, more than 20,000 people gathered outside the U.S. Capitol for a community Christmas celebration featuring a 40-foot Norway spruce.
 The program included the U.S. Marine Band, a chorus of 1,000 local singers, Christmas carols, nativity scenes, and Boy Scouts carrying American flags.
 A lighted display proclaimed “Peace on Earth. Good Will to Men.”
 Similar community celebrations continued in the years that followed, laying the groundwork for the nationally recognized ceremony established in 1923.
 Although the two events were different, they shared a common purpose: bringing people together through music, Christmas traditions, and a brightly decorated tree.
 Music and Celebration Planned for December 3 
 The 2026 National Christmas Tree Lighting Ceremony will feature performances by several nationally known entertainers.
 Jessie James Decker will host and perform, joined by Gloria Gaynor, Dustin Lynch, Gretchen Wilson, Julia Cole, and LOCASH.
 Military performers, including the U.S. Army Downrange and U.S. Navy Sea Chanters, will also participate.
 This year’s program will celebrate America’s 250th anniversary, featuring music and traditions connected to the country’s history.
 The National Park Service and National Park Foundation organized the ceremony.
 Attendance at the December 3 ceremony requires tickets, which were distributed through a free lottery. The lottery closed November 4, and winners were notified November 12.
 However, visitors do not need tickets to enjoy the National Christmas Tree display after the lighting ceremony.
 Free Public Viewing Begins December 5 
 The tree will be open for public viewing beginning Saturday, December 5.
 The National Christmas Tree site is located on the Ellipse in President’s Park, south of the White House.
 Admission to the display is free.
 The National Christmas Tree is traditionally surrounded by smaller decorated trees representing states, territories, and other participating communities.
 The accompanying America Celebrates display features ornaments created by students, giving young people an opportunity to share their artistic talents and local traditions with visitors from across the country.
 For families planning a holiday visit to Washington, the National Christmas Tree offers an opportunity to enjoy Christmas lights in one of the country’s best-known historic settings.
 Visitors can also combine the display with visits to the National Mall, the Washington Monument, and other nearby attractions.
 A Little Piece of Virginia at Christmas 
 For Highland County, the selection is an opportunity to share the region’s character with a national audience.
 The county is known for its quiet mountain valleys, forests, scenic landscapes, and rural traditions.
 This Christmas, one of its native red spruce trees will stand near the White House, surrounded by holiday lights and visited by families from across the nation.
 Cline said he hopes visitors will appreciate the tree’s Virginia origins.
 “As families across the Nation gather to celebrate Christmas, I hope they take a moment to appreciate that a little piece of Virginia will help to make this holiday season special,” he said.
 From a mountain forest in Highland County to the heart of the nation’s capital, this year’s National Christmas Tree will carry a piece of Virginia’s natural heritage into a celebration that has united communities for more than a century.
 The 2026 National Christmas Tree Lighting Ceremony is December 3, and free public viewing begins December 5.
 Additional information is available at www.thenationaltree.org and through the National Park Service .
